solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Tongue poke – pain is it? (6,5)

blocks.note: a tongue is a language, here French
to poke is to stick (a finger in)

annotation.surface: Someone wonders whether a jab in the tongue is what is hurting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pain' is not the English ache but the French word for bread, and a French stick is a baguette, so the definition speaks the very tongue the wordplay names.
annotation.definitionFit: Pain is French for bread, and a French stick is the long loaf.

clue.text: Turner Prize work stolen to order, every second counting (5)

indicators.note: only the second letter of each word is counted

blocks.note: second letters of pRize, wOrk, sTolen, tO, oRder

annotation.surface: A prize-winning artwork is lifted by a thief working on commission.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turner Prize' reads as the famous art award, but the capital is only camouflage: 'Turner' is the definition, something that turns.
annotation.definitionFit: A rotor is the part of a machine that turns.

clue.text: Care where English Channel has flowed uphill (7)

indicators.note: in a down clue, going uphill means reading from the bottom up

blocks.note: E = English
a rut is a channel or groove
has run = has flowed

annotation.surface: A worried note about water from the English Channel running the wrong way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'English Channel' looks like the sea between England and France; it splits into E and a rut.
annotation.definitionFit: To nurture is to care for; the nouns match too.

clue.text: Race is one short of a football team? (6)

blocks.note: read as possession: a side a player down has only so many

blocks.clueFragment: one short of a football team
blocks.note: a football team has eleven players; one short is ten

annotation.surface: A question about whether a contest is a player down.
annotation.walkthrough: Read the answer as HAS TEN: a side that has ten is one short of the eleven a football team fields.
annotation.definitionFit: To hasten is to race, both verbs of hurrying.

clue.text: Figure, strangely integral (8)

indicators.note: the letters are arranged strangely

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: A mathematician notes that a number or shape is oddly essential.
annotation.walkthrough: The maths-flavoured surface makes 'integral' look like calculus; it is only letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: figure in the geometric sense, and the three-sided shape is one.

clue.text: Gear filling blocks with helium (7)

indicators.note: helium fills the blocks, sitting inside them

blocks.note: clots = blocks, as in a blood vessel
He is the chemical symbol for helium

annotation.surface: Equipment that stuffs building blocks with helium, like a party balloon kit.
annotation.walkthrough: The helium goes in just before the last letter of the blocks; the party-balloon surface hides a wardrobe.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain, casual synonym for what you wear.

clue.text: Source of information US president once put on paper (4,9)

blocks.note: either George Bush
the Daily Telegraph newspaper

annotation.surface: A former American president makes it into the newspaper as a source.
annotation.walkthrough: The bush telegraph is the informal grapevine by which news spreads; a setter for the Telegraph naming its own paper is a small in-joke.
annotation.definitionFit: The bush telegraph, the grapevine, is where rumour and news come from.

clue.text: Great improvisation of Monroe, American (8)

indicators.note: the letters are improvised into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder
US = American

annotation.surface: Praise for Marilyn Monroe, the American star, ad-libbing brilliantly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Great' looks like praise of the performance, but it is the definition of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Great, in the sense of very large, is enormous.

clue.text: Politician identified as criminal, effectively working on plot? (5-8)

blocks.note: a Green is a member of the Green Party
to finger someone is to identify them to the police

annotation.surface: A politician is exposed as a crook who was scheming all along.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plot' looks like a conspiracy, fitting the criminal politician; it is a garden plot, and the question mark flags the twist.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone green-fingered gardens well, working a plot effectively.

clue.text: Perfect and articulate (5)

blocks.note: perfect in the sense of complete, as in a perfect stranger
articulate as a verb: to say

annotation.walkthrough: Both words look like adjectives; the second is the verb, as in articulating a sound.
annotation.definitionFit: Perfect and utter both mean complete, as in a perfect stranger; articulate and utter both mean say.

clue.text: Big fish at sea in prison when virtually bankrupt (9)

indicators.note: virtually means almost all, so the last letter goes
bankrupt means broken, so the letters are broken up

blocks.note: PRISONWHEN without its final N

annotation.surface: A tycoon ends up behind bars when the money has nearly run out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Big fish' is slang for an important person, and at sea places them in shipping, so the definition is not a whale.
annotation.definitionFit: A shipowner is a big fish, a person of importance, in the maritime world.

clue.text: 8 Down that man, unclear if wobbly (9)

indicators.note: wobbly letters are unsteady, out of place

blocks.note: he = that man
anagram of UNCLEAR

annotation.surface: A man described as enormous but shaky and vague.
annotation.walkthrough: 8 Down is ENORMOUS, so the definition is another word for huge.
annotation.definitionFit: Herculean, like the labours of Hercules, means enormous.

clue.text: Charger for example plugged into watch, or separate (5)

indicators.note: the answer is plugged into the words that follow

blocks.note: watcH OR SEparate

annotation.surface: Instructions for a phone charger: plug it into your smartwatch or keep them apart.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Charger' is the device you plug into a watch; here it is a warhorse.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a charger is a cavalry mount, one kind of the animal.

clue.text: Book location in Greater Manchester (6)

blocks.note: the abbreviation of an Old Testament book
a town just west of Manchester, in north-west England, known for its currant cakes

annotation.surface: A booking for a venue somewhere in Greater Manchester.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb, to reserve a place; it is the abbreviated Bible book. Eccles is also the home of the Eccles cake.
annotation.definitionFit: Eccles abbreviates Ecclesiastes and is also a town in Greater Manchester.

clue.text: Arrangement of locks: in remedy one breaks out (8)

indicators.note: the pieces go in the remedy
one breaks into out, splitting it

blocks.note: a cure is a remedy
off = out, as a light is off
I = one, the Roman numeral

annotation.surface: A locksmith's puzzle: the fix for a jail lock, where one prisoner escapes.
annotation.walkthrough: Two containers nest: the one sits inside the out, and that pair sits inside the remedy after its first letter. 'Locks' is hair, not door fittings.
annotation.definitionFit: A hairdresser's word, borrowed from French, for a styled head of hair.

clue.text: Great time on holiday, when mission begins (5-3)

definitions.note: the definition is a clause for a moment; the answer is the noun naming it

blocks.note: a blast is a great time, a party
off work = on holiday

annotation.surface: A fun break away before the real job starts.
annotation.walkthrough: The mission is a space launch, and blast-off is the moment it begins.
annotation.definitionFit: Blast-off is the launch, the moment a space mission begins.

clue.text: Try and catch of course! (4,4)

blocks.note: a judge tries, or hears, a case
to catch what someone says is to hear it

annotation.surface: Someone asked to attempt a catch replies that naturally they will.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Try' and 'catch' look like rugby and cricket; both are the courtroom and listening senses of hear. 'Hear, hear!' is the cry of agreement in Parliament.
annotation.definitionFit: Hear, hear! shouts agreement, just as 'of course!' does.

clue.text: Delinquent? I have backed older miscreant (8)

indicators.note: backed means turned back, read in reverse
a miscreant misbehaves, so the letters of older are out of line

blocks.note: I've = I have
anagram of OLDER

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether a young offender has turned their back on an older villain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Miscreant' at the end looks like the definition, a noun for a wrongdoer; it is the anagram indicator, and the definition is 'Delinquent', used as a noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a delinquent, as a noun, is a wrongdoer.

clue.text: Derbyshire river drained away after chestnut uprooted (7)

indicators.note: went comes after the chestnut
in a down clue, uprooted means pulled upward, so read upward

blocks.note: chestnut is a reddish-brown colour
the water went = the water drained away

annotation.surface: A river in Derbyshire dries up after a chestnut tree falls into it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chestnut' looks like the tree, fitting 'uprooted'; it is the colour. The Derwent is a river in Derbyshire, a county in central England.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional fact: it is the county's main river, flowing south from the Peak District to join the Trent.

clue.text: Ultimately, college don is stupid – creative mind? (6)

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter
stupid letters are senseless, jumbled

blocks.note: last letter of collegE
anagram of DON IS

annotation.surface: A student's verdict: the college lecturer is dim, or a creative genius?
annotation.walkthrough: Thomas Edison, the prolific inventor, is the creative mind; the question mark marks a definition by example.
annotation.definitionFit: Edison, the inventor, is a famous example of a creative mind.

clue.text: Loot polished off where last of cash spent (7)

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so the letters are jumbled
last of takes the final letter of cash
that letter is spent, used up and gone

blocks.note: POLISHED without the H
last letter of casH, the letter removed

annotation.surface: Thieves finish off the job once the final money has gone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Polished off' reads as a phrase meaning finished; here 'polished' is the fodder and 'off' the anagram indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to plunder a place.

clue.text: Frightful cast, not as honest (6)

indicators.note: not as means without the letters AS

blocks.note: dire = frightful
CAST with AS removed

annotation.surface: A verdict on a play: the cast was terrible, and not as truthful as they seemed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Frightful cast' reads as a bad acting company; it splits into DIRE and a reduced CAST.
annotation.definitionFit: Direct means frank and straightforward, which is honest.

clue.text: 22 Down, in both directions? (5)

indicators.note: the answer reads the same forwards and backwards

blocks.note: a word that reads the same forwards and backwards

annotation.walkthrough: 22 Down is DIRECT, used here as a verb: to direct someone to a source is to refer them. The pun is that 'both directions' also names the palindrome.
annotation.definitionFit: To direct someone to a person or place is to refer them there.

clue.text: Welcome back nation that’s passed check (9)

indicators.note: the nation has passed the check, so it comes after it

blocks.note: to rein in is to check
a state is a nation

annotation.surface: A country cleared through border control is greeted home.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a passport check; 'passed' means gone beyond, so the nation comes after the check.
annotation.definitionFit: To reinstate someone is to welcome them back to a former post.

clue.text: Love a way in, did you say? (5)

indicators.note: asks what was heard, so the answer is a sound-alike

blocks.note: a door is a way in

annotation.surface: Someone mishears a lover's phrase and asks for it to be repeated.
annotation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent, 'a door' and 'adore' sound the same.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, the verb in its stronger sense of loving deeply.

clue.text: Keep going, by challenging (9)

blocks.note: per = by, as in per post
a severe test is a challenging one

annotation.surface: Encouragement to carry on, however hard the going.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'by challenging' look like a manner of keeping going; the two words are separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to carry on despite difficulty.

clue.text: Figure from Sydney? Heavens above! (5)

blocks.note: Oz = Australia, home of Sydney
one is a figure, a number

annotation.surface: An exclamation of surprise at some character from Sydney.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heavens above!' reads as an exclamation; taken literally it points to the ozone layer high in the sky.
annotation.definitionFit: A literal reading: the layer of that gas sits high in the sky, in the heavens above.

clue.text: Narrator, person banking on lie (5-6)

indicators.note: in an across clue, on means placed after

blocks.note: a story is a lie, a fib
a bank teller handles deposits

annotation.surface: A narrator, and someone who is counting on a falsehood.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Banking on' looks like relying on; 'banking' describes the teller and 'on' puts that person after STORY.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: one who tells a tale narrates it.
